content.intro: In this lesson, you will study probabilistic Models within Supervised Learning in Detail. You will connect the syllabus topics below to a small, inspectable example and practice stating what the evidence does—and does not—support.

content_blocks.title: The central idea
content_blocks.text: Probabilistic classifiers combine prior assumptions and evidence to estimate class likelihoods. Check calibration and data assumptions; an output score should not be interpreted as a guarantee of correctness.

content_blocks.title: Syllabus topics covered in this lesson

items.title: Bayes' theorem in classification
items.text: Bayes’ theorem updates a prior belief using the likelihood of observed evidence to compute a posterior. Be explicit about the event, evidence, and base rate; a high likelihood ratio does not erase a very small prior probability.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: 1. Identify what probabilistic models takes as input and what result or decision it is intended to support. 2. Read the example before running it and predict the output. 3. Run the small example, compare actual and expected output, then change one input or assumption and repeat. 4. Record what the example demonstrates and what it does not demonstrate about a real system.

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: If the output differs, check indentation and spelling, confirm you saved the intended file, and compare each input value with the example. If the example runs as expected, do not infer that it proves a trained model works; this snippet is a deterministic teaching aid. Keep sensitive data out of tests.

content_blocks.title: Check before you trust a result
content_blocks.text: This is a small, deterministic teaching example—not a trained AI model or evidence of production performance. Run it with a local Python 3 interpreter; do not paste secrets or private data into experiments.

content.task: Try it yourself: build a tiny synthetic dataset for probabilistic models, establish a simple baseline, and define a suitable metric before looking at results. Separate development decisions from final evaluation and describe one important error.
